Hi Lucinda,

I haven't fully delved into your code, but in my experience, this error usually indicates that your inits don't match your model in terms of the dimensions of the object in question (in this case, psiAB). For example, this might happen if you specify a vector in the inits but then try to use the object as a matrix in the model; or if your object is initialized as a vector with length N, but then you try to refer to a position greater than N in the vector within the model. In this case, I'm not sure if dim(marr)[2]-1 will equal n.occasions-1 - but if so, what I've described probably isn't your problem, unless I've missed something.

I also noticed that you've specified the "inits" object twice - could that be a problem?

inits <- function(){list(phiA = runif(dim(marr)[2]-1, 0, 1),phiB = runif(dim(marr)[2]-1, 0, 1),psiAB = runif(dim(marr)[2]-1, 0, 1))}

inits <- function(){list(psiAB = runif(dim(marr)[2]-1, 0, 1))}

I guess psiAB is specified identically in both of them, so perhaps that doesn't explain why there is an error relating to psiAB. But phiA and phiB are missing in the second line (which is what will beused) so maybe that has some downstream effects...?

If that doesn't help, I'll take a closer look later, or perhaps someone else will beat me to it.

messages.body_plain:
If V becomes a vector, then you would need to specify an integer in the data (say, T) that is the maximum number of surveys (what V is in your code right now). The dimensions of y are [N, T], and you just replace the NA’s with 0’s because Stan won’t accept NA. The dimensions for Wmat also become [N, T], and T gets used in the transformed parameters section.

I looked back at my old code, and realized the specification of V[i] actually goes in the likelihood. That way, when the model evaluates the likelihood it ignores the surveys that weren’t done.

This works fine for me. If any Stan experts out there know why it shouldn’t I’d be interested to know.

After fiddling with your code a little bit I got it to work with my missing survey data. A quick look should show you where the changes were made.

data {

  int<lower=1> N; //indicates that the variable is an integer with smallest value = 0

  int<lower=1> V[N]; //number of visits

  int<lower=1> T; // The maximum number of surveys done at a station

  int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N,T]; //presence absence data

  vector[N] Xmat; // X variable

  real Wmat[N, T]; // W matrix - detection covariates

parameters {

  vector[2] beta;  //occupancy slope params

  vector[2] alpha;  //detection slope params

}

transformed parameters {

  vector[N] psi; // prob of of occurrence

  real pij[N, T]; // prob of detection

  //calculate psi_i and pij

  for (isite in 1:N){

    psi[isite] = inv_logit( beta[1] + Xmat[isite]*beta[2] );

    for (ivisit in 1:T){

      pij[isite, ivisit] = inv_logit( alpha[1] + Wmat[isite, ivisit]*alpha[2] );

    }

  }

}

model {

  // local variables to avoid recomputing log(psi) and log(1-psi)

  vector[N] log_psi;

  vector[N] log1m_psi;

  for (isite in 1:N) {

    log_psi[isite] = log(psi[isite]);

    log1m_psi[isite] = log1m(psi[isite]);

  }

  // priors

  alpha ~ normal(0, 1000);

  beta ~ normal(0, 1000);

  // likelihood

  for (isite in 1:N) {

    if (sum(y[isite]) > 0){

      target += log_psi[isite] + bernoulli_lpmf(y[isite, 1:V[isite]]|pij[isite, 1:V[isite]]) ;

    }else {

      target += log_sum_exp(log_psi[isite] + bernoulli_lpmf(y[isite, 1:V[isite]]|pij[isite, 1:V[isite]]),log1m_psi[isite]);

    }

  }//end likelihood contribution

}

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I just constructed a model (modification of Jolly Seber) which models
everything - population growth, survival and recruitment. It is from a
single data source - Constant Effort Sites ringing scheme and I am
about to publish it. Now I wonder: is such a model classified as an
Integrated Population Model?

What precisely the "Integrated" means in this term?

1) Does it mean that more data sets are integrated in one model?

or

2) Does it mean that all demographic information is integrated into
single, complete and comprehensive population equation (N[t] = some
function of N[t-1]) including all demographic parameters?

My model clearly does not comply with 1, since it is only from single
data source, but it does comply with 2 - it does integrate all
information possible. So, I now need to know if I should present my
model as IPM or something else.

Thanks a lot!

Tomas

Hi Tomas,

This is an interesting discussion.  I would say that you need at least 1 other data source that provides information on a population process for it to be an IPM, even if those data come from the same population (same individuals even).  This would distinguish an individual attribute like body size from something like litter size (# offspring) -- the former can be incorporated into capture-recapture but does not necessarily inform a population process like the latter does.

Just my debatable opinion of course, interested to see what others think.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Tomas, and hello Dan,

of course, 'integrated' is just a buzz-word, some might say. However, the way the term has come to be used in the literature in the context of IPMs, it is exactly what Dan says: you need at least two different data sources. And what's more, my colleague Michael Schaub (e.g., in the Review paper with Fitsum Abadie, around 2011) defines integrated population models as population models that are fit to at least two types of independent data sources: one of which must be a time series of population counts and the other one a data set that more directly informs about demographic rates such as survival, e.g., a capture-recapture data set.

In a more general sense, we can recognize that 'integrated models' are one of the main developmental branches of all of ecological statistics: the field is FULL with new models where people find a model-based way of combining different data sets that inform on the same underlying process. In the context of hierarchical models, this almost always means that there is a shared process model, but different observation models for the different data sets.

Best regards ---- Marc

In case this can be of use to anyone else (or someone can improve on it!), I'm reactivating this thread to share my adaptation of Richard's trick (thanks!) to a simple POPAN model with data augmentation. As far as I was able to work out, the shortcut isn't as clean in this context, so it only provided 10-20% time savings in my JAGS simulations. Model data and inits (appended below) were adapted accordingly based on Richard's code.

I rewrote the following likelihood (from Kery and Schaub):

 # Likelihood
 for (i in 1:M){
    # First occasion
    # State process
    w[i] ~ dbern(psi)   # Draw latent inclusion
    z[i,1] ~ dbern(nu[1])
    # Observation process
    mu1[i] <- p[i,1] * z[i,1] * w[i]
    y[i,1] ~ dbern(mu1[i])
    # Subsequent occasions
    for (t in 2:n.occasions){
       # State process
       q[i,t-1] <- 1-z[i,t-1]
       mu2[i,t] <- phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1] + nu[t] * prod(q[i,1:(t-1)])
       z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu2[i,t])
       # Observation process
       mu3[i,t] <- z[i,t] * p[i,t] * w[i]
       y[i,t] ~ dbern(mu3[i,t])
    } #t
 } #i

as:

# Likelihood
for (i in 1:M){
   # First occasion
   # State process
   w[i] ~ dbern(psi)  # Draw latent inclusion
   z[i,1] ~ dbern(nu[1])
   # Subsequent occasions
   for (t in 2:n.occasions){
      # State process
      q[i,t-1] <- 1-z[i,t-1]
      mu2[i,t] <- phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1] + nu[t] * prod(q[i,1:(t-1)])
      z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu2[i,t])
   } #t
} #i

for (i in 1:n0){
   for (t in 1:n.occasions){
      y[i,t] ~ dbern(p[i,t] * z[i,t] * w[i])
   } #t
} #i
for(i in (n0+1):M) {
   for (t in 1:n.occasions){
      pzo[i,t] <- 1 - p[i,t] * z[i,t] * w[i]    # probability of not being detected on each occasion
   }
   zeros[i] ~ dbern(1-prod(pzo[i,]))    # probability of at least one detection
}

inits <- function(){list(z=z.init, w=w.init)}

> > > > >
> > > > >

messages.body_plain:
Dear group,

this is perhaps a somewhat off-topic question, but I ask anyway. --- With a colleague we have been musing about the interest to educate the public about basic processes underlying population dynamics, e.g., how things like (initial) population size and the BIDE rates affect outcomes like population trajectories and extinction probabilities and how factors such as (for instance) hunting or wind turbines  on the one hand, or habitat or population management can affect all of these.

We were first thinking about physical models, e.g., using balls in an urn, but I think this is too limited. So the obvious choice is some computer model of a population, where BIDE rates can be specified. Ideally, we’d have some GUI where the user could use a slide bar to set the desired values for the BIDE rates and then there would be one or more plots, e.g., of the trajectory of a single population or of the cluster of such trajectories to show the uncertainty arising from variability or a histogram of final population sizes including an estimate of extinction probability.

I bet somebody has already coded up such solutions and hence, rather than re-invent the wheel, we’d be happy to hear about anything you might know of (or have programmed yourself).

Thank you and best regards  ---- Marc

Hi Marc,

This past spring I was looking for a similar tool for teaching an undergraduate population ecology class. I ended up coding several mini web applications using R and Shiny <https://shiny.rstudio.com/>, which is simple to do and allows you to create something customized to your needs. For example, I wrote this app <https://amtucker.shinyapps.io/wild4890_pred_prey/> (https://amtucker.shinyapps.io/wild4890_pred_prey/) to have students explore predator-prey dynamics. This app <https://amtucker.shinyapps.io/wild4890_pva/> (https://amtucker.shinyapps.io/wild4890_pva/) sounds close to what you are looking for, but it was designed to teach about conducting demographic PVAs and the types of uncertainty involved, so it might contain more detail than you need. You are welcome to use it, and I'm also happy to send along the source code, which is just R wrapped in some special functions to create the web interface.

I hope this helps!
Anna

That is great stuff and should be used much more than just publishing equations.

Another software package that can perform such interactive demonstrations that runs locally (on PC, Mac, and Linux platforms) is Mathematica (Wolfram, Inc.).  Here is an example:  http://demonstrations.wolfram.com/PredatorPreyDynamicsWithTypeTwoFunctionalResponse/.  Attached is a screenshot.

To view such demonstrations it takes a free CDF (computable document format) reader but to buy Mathematica to build such apps is not cheap.  The advantage is that the app runs locally on your machine and can be very responsive.

Jim Baldwin
